subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTINUED OPERATION OF HOWE SOUND COMPANY

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTINUED OPERATION OF HOWE SOUND COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to inform the house that an arrangement has been worked out under which the directors of the Howe Sound Mining Company have agreed to keep the Britannia mine open on a reduced operating basis for a further period, which it is hoped will be at least six months. The parties to the arrangement are the dominion government, the government of British Columbia, the company and the mine workers. I am informed that a telegram has accordingly been sent from New York this morning to the mine management at Britannia.
As the house knows, for some weeks we have been holding discussions with the company, the men and the provincial government to see what could be done to avoid a shutdown of the mine with the disastrous consequence which would follow for the 700 men and their families who would have been thrown out of work as a result. It should be emphasized in fairness to the company that at no time have they ever either directly or indirectly sought governmental assistance or intervention. They have, however, shown throughout a highly commendable readiness to postpone a shut-down which their own experts urged them to make in order to carry on discussions in an effort to arrive at a solution which will keep the men at work notwithstanding that they were and still are incurring substantial losses.
At the time these discussions commenced the hope was to keep all the men at work. However, on December 3 the company advised that a further recommendation had been received from their consultants, as a result of which their directors had no option but to decide that it would be in effect an abuse of their property and a breach of their responsibility as directors to continue full scale mining operations under present conditions. We were, therefore, faced with a decision of the company that, effective today, these operations would be discontinued.
They were prepared, however, to consider an arrangement to continue operating on a
reduced scale if some assistance were forthcoming. This arrangement involves a complete reorganization of their operations, but will provide for the continued employment of between 350 and 400 personnel.
Although we were naturally disappointed that it was no longer possible to keep all the men at work, it was still most desirable to do everything possible to keep something over half of them in employment. I am very happy to be able to say that this has now been achieved.
The company has agreed, on the assurance that the assistance detailed later will be forthcoming, that it will reorganize its operations and continue work on the property in order to provide employment for between 350 and 400 personnel, thus avoiding a lay-off of the whole working force at a time of year when it would be virtually impossible for them to secure alternative work.
A substantial part of the company's operating cost is incurred in the expense of operation and maintenance of their townsite and the provision of services to the houses occupied by their employees, all of which are owned by the company. It is our thought, therefore, that the contribution of government should be founded on the basis of assistance in meeting these costs of supplying and servicing accommodation. On this basis, it has been agreed that if the two governments will provide a total of $20,000 per month for up to six months the company will continue its operations on the reduced scale referred to, and will continue to provide accommodation for the 350 to 400 personnel employed for such period as may be practicable.
As regards the amount of assistance to be provided by each government, it has been agreed that, if parliament approves, 80 per cent will be paid by the dominion government and 20 per cent by the government of British Columbia. I should say that the exact figure of percentage is subject to confirmation which we expect to receive very shortly, but it will be very close to the figure I have just mentioned. The men have already made, and will continue to make, a substantial contribution toward helping to solve this problem. The company will continue to incur substantial losses in the immediate future.
The government recognizes that what is proposed is unusual, but this is an unusual situation. Here is an industry in an isolated

Labour Conditions
locality, all of whose workers live in a company-operated and company-owned town. If the mine were to close now, not only would the employees be unable at this time of year to secure alternative employment but they and their families would be without accommodation. It is true that the plan which is proposed to keep the mine open for a few months involves only about one-half the workers, but it may nevertheless be possible -and this has yet to be worked out-to find some method of providing winter accommodation during the remainder of these winter months for those who unfortunately will have to be released from work.
This plan will thus not only maintain men and their families in employment and accommodation over the winter months when there would otherwise be no hope of finding alternatives for either, but also marks a unique co-operative effort to find a solution to a pressing problem, with contributions being made from four sources; the two governments, the men and the company.
With regard to the company, I should like to emphasize that for the last several months the mine has been operating at a loss of between $60,000 and $80,000 a month. Even with the assistance now to be provided and work being continued on a reduced scale, losses will continue to be substantial. It seems to me that the board of directors and the management are due a sincere expression of gratitude for their contribution in agreeing to keep the mine open under these conditions.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, the government will in the very near future be submitting a specific proposal to parliament to authorize the payment of $16,000 a month, or such other proportionate amount as will finally be agreed to with the province of British Columbia, toward defraying a portion of the costs of keeping the Britannia mine open for a period of up to six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONTINUED OPERATION OF HOWE SOUND COMPANY

If the price of copper should rise, then I would assume that the need for assistance will be proportionately lessened, but that would be a matter for further negotiation.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday last the hon. members for Burnaby-Coquitlam and Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare raised the matter as to which provinces had signed agreements with the federal government to provide for the recent increases in old age assistance benefits. I am now in a position to give the house the following information.
Seven provinces have signed agreements, effective November 1, 1957, with the federal government in connection with increases in benefits provided not only under the Old Age Assistance Act but also under the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act. These provinces are British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I have been informed that four of these seven provinces- New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan-actually paid the increased benefits in November. Another, Nova Scotia, apparently provided the increases in some cases, but the majority will be paid later with effect, of course, from November 1. I might point out that since these three programs are administered by the provinces, the latter have the responsibility for deciding when the increases are actually implemented.

As far as the remaining provinces are concerned, my department has received a verbal communication from the province of Quebec indicating its intention to share in the increased payments under these programs, and Newfoundland has also telegraphed its agreement. We have as yet received no communication from Prince Edward Island in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. There are two projects in mind for the city of St. John's.
One project consists of 46 subsidized housing units, which is to be built on land in the central area of the city which has been cleared with the aid of a federal grant of $15,000 under section 23 of the National Housing Act. The site is part of a larger area which has been earmarked for redevelopment.
The other project consists of approximately 155 subsidized rental housing units. Tenders were called late in 1956. One bid only was received. It was rejected, as it was too high in relation to the original estimate. Ever since that time further proceeding with respect to those two projects has been withheld at the request of the government of Newfoundland.

speechtext: I would like to address a question to the Minister of Transport, a copy of which was sent to him yesterday. Could the minister advise the house as to any proposed shipbuilding program presently planned by the Department of Transport, and as to when such a program will become operative?

speechtext: Order paper.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CURRENT SHIPBUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice yesterday of his intention to ask this question, and I have the following reply:
Early in January we are going to call for tenders for the construction of six ships totalling in cost approximately $10 million. These will be as follows: A supply and buoy vessel, also fitted to carry out search and rescue work, for use on the west coast. A supply and buoy vessel, also designed for icebreaking, to be used on the Atlantic coast, gulf of St. Lawrence, northern and other waters where necessary.
Two supply and buoy vessels to replace existing ships at present on duty in the maritimes. A lightship for the St. Lawrence river. A work vessel and tug for use by the St. Lawrence ship channel division.
In addition to the foregoing new construction, the Department of Transport will also call for tenders early in January for the conversion of two L.C.T.8's to fit them for

the transportation and handling of dry cargo and bulk fuel for the Foxe basin D.E.W. line sites. At present one of these vessels is in the maritimes and the other on the St. Lawrence. The approximate cost of converting these two vessels is expected to be about $1 million. Also, about the end of the first week in February my department will call for tenders for the construction of a small ferry to operate between Pelee island and the mainland.
I should like to add that the labour content of these projects I have just listed is approximately 3i million man hours for Canadian workers. Contracts should be let about five to six weeks after tender calls, that is during February, for all but one of these vessels, and orders for materials and other work placed immediately thereafter. In placing contracts, account will be taken of the desirability of spreading this work among various shipyards, and of the promptness with which the work can be undertaken by the various shipyards so as to assist winter employment.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    STATEMENT AS TO SAFETY PRECAUTIONS DURING TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to an inquiry directed to the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce on Saturday by the hon. member for Port Arthur as to safety precautions observed during the testing of the Trans-Canada pipe line.
The board of transport commissioners advise that the testing on the Trans-Canada pipe line is made in accordance with section 8 of the American standard code of pressure piping, which requires that during tests suitable steps shall be taken to keep persons not working on the testing operations out of the testing area, and the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company had adopted the policy of sending their land men ahead of the testing to warn all residents immediately adjacent to the line that they are testing. In cases where people are considered to be living too close to the pipe line for safety the company insists that these people move out until the test has been completed, and pays all bills in connection with their moving.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ASSISTANCE TO FISHERMEN FOLLOWING STORM LOSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, December 5, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare asked a question regarding possible action by the government to assist fishermen who have suffered severe storm damage to their lobster traps. I apologize to the hon. member for straining his patience to this extent and for the long delay in answering, but I think he will understand that some inquiry had to be made on the spot, and that takes time.
Officials of the department have investigated the situation locally and reported the estimated extent of the damage to me. As hon. members are aware, this is a recurring problem and these fishermen have the opportunity of insuring their traps against storm damage under the fishermen's indemnity plan. It is reported that 172 fishermen, representing approximately 18 per cent of the total in the affected area, had taken

Inquiries of the Ministry out this insurance. These fishermen are now making claims which will be given immediate attention. In general, losses appear to have averaged some 30 per cent of traps set, although there has been great variation in this average figure. It is also reported that most fishermen have additional traps which were not in the water when the storms occurred. Thus they will be able to carry on fishing despite their losses.
In view of all these facts the government does not consider it necessary to take special action at this time. Any fisherman wishing to protect himself against future possible losses may take advantage of the insurance offered under the indemnity plan. I might add that no request for such action has been received by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for his courtesy in giving me notice of his question. I replied to a similar question on October 18, as reported at pages 125 and 126 of Hansard of that date; but since that reply I can say now that the Department of Justice is giving serious consideration to this question, along with consideration it is giving to a number of proposals that have been made for amendments to other sections of the Criminal Code.
It is not possible to introduce a bill to amend the Criminal Code at this session of parliament. It may be possible to introduce such a bill at the next session. The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 4, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Green-Mr. Courtemanche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954 to increase from two hundred and fifty million dollars to four hundred million dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act; and also to provide for the reduction of down payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, DOWN PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
When this resolution was before the committee on December 4 I gave certain figures with regard to the amount of loans which had been approved under the agency loan plan. These figures will be found at page 1879 of Hansard. I thought it might be helpful if I brought those figures up to date today before hon. members deal with the resolution.
As of December 13 the total loans approved numbered 11,951, covering 15,456 units. The total amount was $146,072,339. In addition there were potential commitments-this is as of four days ago-amounting to $21,740,000, making a total of $167,812,339. The starts under the agency loan plan as of December 13 were as follows: British Columbia, 288; Alberta, 1,265; Saskatchewan, 258; Manitoba, 349; Ontario, 4,701; Quebec, 1,269; New Brunswick, 80; Nova Scotia, 110; Newfoundland, 10, or a total of 8,330. The branch offices report that construction is starting as quickly as possible after approval and that cancellations are likely to be few in number.
I have figures also by way of comparison of the results under this agency loan plan and under the insured loan plan, which is the normal National Housing Act procedure, for the third quarter of 1957. These figures are as follows. For insured loans, third quarter of 1957, the average income of the borrower was $5,943; the average income under the agency loan plan is $5,003, a decrease of 15.8 per cent. The average down payment under the insured loan plan in the third quarter of 1957 was $3,921; under the agency loan plan it has been $2,548, a decrease of 35 per cent. The average amount of loan under the insured loan, third quarter of this year, was $10,913; the average amount under the agency loan plan was $9,875, a decrease of 9.5 per cent. The average dwelling cost under the insured loan was $14,615 and under the agency loan $12,423, a decrease of 15 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin my remarks by complimenting the minister upon the lucidity of the explanation he gave the other night when this resolution 96698-157
National Housing Act
was first considered by this committee. 1 thought he explained very clearly the objects he had in mind, and no doubt because he was anxious to have the resolution adopted with the minimum of debate he avoided repeating the more controversial statements he made earlier in this session in reply to questions on orders of the day.
I want also to thank him for the generous and complimentary references to his predecessor, Hon. Robert H. Winters. We in the official opposition, and particularly those of us who were associated with Mr. Winters in the previous government, know how sincerely interested he was in the whole question of housing and how fully he devoted his effort and attention to this problem. I believe that some of the statistics to which I should like to refer presently are an eloquent testimonial to the success of the policies for which Mr. Winters was responsible.
I should like to say also to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, how much the members of the official opposition appreciated having an opportunity of discussing the question of housing with Dr. Bates of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and two of his officials. They were good enough to answer many questions which were put to them and they added materially, I think, and I might also say in a very kindly way, to the sum of our knowledge on this subject.
I now come to the resolution before this committee, Mr. Chairman, which hon. members will recall first appeared in Votes and Proceedings on November 25. This, of course, was the first official intimation the members of this committee had of the intention of the government to introduce amendments to the National Housing Act. I should like to point out, however, that the Solicitor General had, as early as November 8, publicly announced outside this house the government's decision to present a bill to encourage the building of new houses. Having for so long listened to Conservative members who claimed that under the last government the rights of parliament were being ignored, and recalling the numerous Conservative promises to restore parliament to its former greatness, I can only say now that I am much surprised that the first announcement of this legislation was made, not in the speech from the throne, not in Votes and Proceedings, but in an address made in Montreal nearly three weeks before this resolution appeared on the order paper.
The words the Solicitor General used on that occasion are not without interest. I shall read from he Devoir of November 9 an extract from the report of his speech. Here is what he is reported as having said, and

National Housing Act
as it is in French, but I shall translate it so the minister will fully appreciate the significance of his colleague's remarks:
(Translation):
The hon. Minister of Public Works is shortly to introduce a bill which, according to the Hon. Mr. Balcer, will promote home building. The Minister of Finance, on his part, is said to have in mind another bill which would settle the matter of interest rate and facilitate the borrowing of money.
(Text):
As there is no simultaneous translation, Mr. Chairman, I shall translate his words as follows:
The Minister of Public Works will shortly present a bill which-according to the Hon. Balcer-will encourage the building of houses.
I point out to the Minister of Public Works that his colleague was just about three weeks ahead of him in making this news public. But then, Mr. Chairman while that is what the Solicitor General said of the measure now under consideration, he also continued as follows:
The Minister of Finance, on his part, has in mind another bill which would settle the question of the rate of interest and facilitate the borrowing of money.
This last item is a most interesting bit of news, and as the matter is very closely related to the subject of this resolution on housing, I hope the Minister of Public Works, before this debate is concluded, will advise the committee more fully as to the project announced by the Solicitor General on the occasion to which I have just referred. The minister himself, in his explanation of the purposes of this resolution, said nothing either with regard to the rate of interest or with regard to any further legislation to facilitate the borrowing of money.
The presentation of this resolution affords an opportunity for a review of what has been accomplished under the legislation which it is now proposed to amend. I feel that for this purpose I should go back to the time when the National Housing Act was adopted in 1954. I have no intention of reviewing all that was said at that time but I think I might quote what was then said by Mr. Winters in presenting the resolution on which the National Housing Act was based. As reported at page 998 of Hansard for 1953-54 he said this:
The main object of the legislation is to broaden the supply of mortgage money by making that form of investment more attractive, increasing the number of lenders and making more funds available for mortgage lending.
Before coming to examine the extent to which this object has been achieved I should like to remind hon. members of the fact that mortgage lending in Canada has always suffered from a peculiar disability. I may add that I speak of the matter in the light of some
[Mr. Marler.l
personal experience, having been closely connected with mortgage lending in Montreal during the approximately 30 years I practised law before becoming a member of this parliament.
The peculiar disability to which I have just referred is that in good times industry, using the term in the broadest sense of the word, competes actively for the investor's capital and offers a more negotiable security than a mortgage on a house, while in bad times builders are not anxious to undertake the construction of large numbers of houses, buyers are scarcer and the demand for mortgage money falls off. It is in the light of this competition for the investor's dollar that we may now take a look at what took place after the National Housing Act came into operation early in 1954.
Hon. members will recall that under the former legislation it was the practice for joint loans to be made by the lending institutions and C.M.H.C., that is to say the major part of the funds were advanced by the lending institutions and only a smaller part by C.M.H.C. itself. Upon the introduction of the new act joint loans were abandoned, and a plan under which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would insure the mortgage loans made under the act by the lending institutions was substituted for it. In this way a National Housing Act mortgage was made more attractive as a form of investment, more secure and incidentally more easily negotiable.
Moreover, by adding the chartered banks to the list of approved lenders not only was the number of lenders significantly increased, but a substantial volume of additional funds was made available for mortgage lending.
I think most objective people would fully agree that the main object stated by the former minister has been achieved during the period which has elapsed since the act came into operation, because it is a fact that in that period both the volume of new residential construction and the amount of mortgage lending on new housing have attained unprecedently high levels. Up to the end of 1952 the number of new dwellings started in any one year had only once exceeded 90,000 units. That was in 1950. It was only in 1953 that for the first time the total of new dwellings started exceeding 100,000.
In that year, commitments by lending institutions to make mortgage loans also attained a new high level. Conventional mortgage loans amounted to about $119 million, while loans under the previous National Housing Act amounted to about $314 million, making a rather impressive total of approximately $433 million in all.

Though 1953 was a record year both as to the number of new dwellings started and as to the amount of mortgage commitments made, higher levels were attained in each of the succeeding years 1954, 1955 and 1956 under the housing legislation adopted early in 1954. Thus, according to "Canadian Housing Statistics", published by C.M.H.C., new units were started as follows: in 1954, 113,527; in 1955, 138,276; and in 1956, 127,311. Mortgage commitments were as follows: in 1954, $670.6 million which, Mr. Chairman, I would point out, includes some carry-over from the former practice of making joint loans; 1955, in which the total was $892.4 million or more than twice the record established in 1953, and in 1956 the total reached some $700.1 million.
It does seem to be a fact that the 1954 legislation gave a positive stimulus to the building of new homes. There was a substantial increase in the number of homes financed by means of conventional mortgages but an even greater increase in the number of new homes financed under the new National Housing Act. It is a fact that in 1955, the best year we have known so far, when more than 138,000 new dwelling units were started, over 65,000 were financed under the new legislation.
So that in the circumstances it seems reasonable to point out that the principal purpose of the new legislation to increase the number of houses built each year was fully attained in the three years in question.
I know, of course, that the number of dwellings started in 1957 is below the corresponding period of 1956 and even less than the number started in the peak year of 1955. But I suggest that if a tendency had not developed to look on 1955 and 1956 as normal years for residential construction, the number of starts in this year 1957 would be regarded as fairly satisfactory. It seems abundantly clear that the number would have been larger if there had not been such a strong demand from other borrowers.
But I might say that it was not so very long ago that a good number of people in Canada were wondering whether a continuation of the intensive activity in the building of new homes such as existed in 1955 would not bring about a serious inflation of building costs and indeed of the other costs associated with the building of new homes.
I cannot help thinking that the slowing down in 1957 of the building of new homes, though it may have brought hardship in some quarters, will be considered by fair-minded people as a good thing both for builders and for home owners. There has been a period of consolidation which made it possible for
96698-157i
National Housing Act
home owners who wished to sell their homes to do so on not unsatisfactory terms, and for the development of a more substantial and solid demand for new housing units as they were built.
As I said a moment ago, another purpose of the new legislation was to increase the flow of mortgage funds by widening the group of approved lenders under the act. That this purpose has been fully achieved is demonstrated by the significant contribution that has been made by the chartered banks to the financing of new residential construction. The statistics as to mortgage lending published by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation show that in the period from 1954 to 1956 the banks approved mortgage loans to an aggregate amount of nearly $650 million, to finance the construction of some 67,230 dwelling units. I understand, moreover, that in the current year, the banks are fully carrying out the commitment to lend $150 million to which the former minister of public works referred in the House of Commons early in the present year.
I appreciate, just as do other hon. members, that this is a lower rate of lending than prevailed in 1954 and 1955 when the banks started in this field of investment, but whatever may be the amounts currently being loaned by the banks, even the short experience that the last few years have provided has amply demonstrated the wisdom of authorizing and encouraging the banks to make insured loans under the act and to put at the service of prospective home owners the extensive facilities which the banks have in many centres large and small across Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to overlook the fact that we are at this moment more directly concerned with the question of the amount that may be advanced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act, because this is one of the two objectives of this resolution before the committee. The present authority contained in the act places a limit of $250 million on the amount of these advances, and it is of course the moneys advanced under this authority that are used by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make loans under the National Housing Act when it considers it expedient to do so.
In connection with these loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under section 22 of the act it is interesting to note that in the three years 1954, 1955 and 1956, through loans made under the National Housing Act by lending institutions amounted to more than $1,500 million. Central

National Housing Act
Mortgage and Housing Corporation itself loaned less than $65 million. In other words in that period, in which new high levels of home building were established, the financing of the construction of new dwellings was left almost entirely to the lending institutions, that is to say to the life insurance companies, the trust, loan and other companies, and the chartered banks, and they provided a record volume of mortgage money.
Now, in the first half of 1957, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has played a more active part in mortgage lending, and I understand that as of July 1 about $100 million of the amount authorized by the act had been committed. Since the present gov-ernnment has been in office Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has given further commitments for an aggregate amount of about $150 million, so that as the minister explained the present authority of $250 million has just about been used up. It is only natural, therefore, that further funds should be placed at the disposal of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and of course the purpose of the resolution is to place at its disposal a further amount of $150 million.
Mr. Chairman, to this proposal the official opposition has no objection, because it is obvious that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must not be left in a position of having no funds available for new construction, and accordingly we shall support the resolution which is designed to make possible the continuation of policies laid down in the National Housing Act, which hon. members will recall, was sponsored by the previous Liberal government.
However, I think I should point out to the present government that it would be very unfortunate if it were to create the impression that it is going to assume the responsibility of providing all the funds that are needed for new housing. This is a responsibility which rests upon other shoulders as well, and I hope the government will not in any way discourage other lenders from actively participating in meeting present needs for housing in the same way as they have done in recent years. In fact I might go even further and suggest to the government that it should, in ways which are open to the government to act, endeavour to persuade the lending institutions that this is a function which properly they should discharge.
Before I leave this subject of increasing by $150 million the funds available for loaning by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister another comment made by his colleague the Solicitor General. Le Devoir of November 9 reports his remarks

as follows, and I think I should quote them even if it is necessary to translate them, because I think they are the sort of pearls that should not be lost sight of:
(Translation):
Later, referring to the $150 million recently placed at the disposal of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the speaker stated that these credits would all soon be used up, because there were only $28 million left by now. He said that this was only a palliative, but that the crux of the matter would soon be settled by appropriate legislation.
(Text) :
In substance, what the Solicitor General said in speaking of the $150 million which the government had already placed at the disposal of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was this was only a palliative, but that the crux of the matter, the fundamental problem, would soon be settled by appropriate legislation. Well, I suppose after hearing the words of his colleague the Minister of Public Works will realize that he is just accomplishing a routine formality in asking us to increase these funds by a matter of $150 million, but I hope before the debate is over he will tell us just what further legislation he has in mind to which the Solicitor General's description of "an immediate palliative" would not be considered to apply.

speechtext:
Of course if he were in the house I would be delighted to have him explain just what he meant, because it seems to me this suggestion is that what we are doing at the moment is merely to give the poor patient a shot in the arm, but that what we are really going to do is reset all his bones and bring him to life by some other legislative process. I must say this intrigues me enormously and of course, as I indicated earlier, I am also very much intrigued by the thought which the Solicitor General expressed that the Minister of Finance-who unhappily is absent this afternoon for good reasons, as we all know- actually had in mind doing something to bring down interest rates and also to facilitate the borrowing of money.
I know there are many people who would like to acquire the secret knowledge necessary to have this new facility made available, but perhaps the minister will enlighten us, when he speaks further on this subject today, as to what are the broader plans such as were announced by the Solicitor General.
I now come, Mr. Chairman, to the second object of this resolution, the question of the reduction of down payments. This, as the minister has explained, has to be done by

increasing the amount of the loan, and the minister has told us that instead of the loan amounting to 90 per cent of the first $8,000 of the lending value and 70 per cent of the lending value in excess of that $8,000, the amendment will enable borrowers to obtain a loan amounting to 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value, and 70 per cent of the lending value in excess of that amount.
The minister put on Hansard a table showing the effect on down payments and the change in the ratio between the loan and the lending value, and it appears from that table that the change will reduce the down payment by $400 in the case of a house having a lending value of $10,000 and by $700 in the case of a house having a lending value of $15,000. We shall not oppose this change in the act which will afford some modest relief although I do not think the relief itself is particularly substantial.
It seems to me that the present difficulty with regard to the down payment does not arise from the way in which the amount of the loan is arrived at under the present provisions of the National Housing Act but from the practices that are being followed by lending institutions in their appraisals of the security. I think the statistics published by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation fully bear out this contention. If we examine the statistics we find that the total average estimated cost of a one-storey single family dwelling has risen from $12,479 in the first quarter of 1955 to $14,725 in the second quarter of 1957 but during this same period the average loan under the National Housing Act on this type of house has risen, I think, from $10,147 to $10,900. This means that the down payment, that is the difference between the total cost and the amount loaned, has increased in the space of 27 months from $2,332 to $3,825, a jump of nearly $1,500. If I understood correctly the figures which the minister gave earlier this afternoon they would seem to show that this difference between the cost of a single family dwelling financed under the N.H.A. and the amount of the loan is now about $3,925.
I am going to leave those figures because I have not had an opportunity of digesting them but the point I would like to emphasize is that although the cost figures which are given in table 49, which table gives the building costs, are figures submitted by the applicant himself. I fully realize that he may be prone sometimes to exaggerate his costs, but leaving out this factor of understandable exaggeration I would like to say, from my own experience with lending institutions, that ever since the National Housing
National Housing Act
Act was first adopted they have followed very conservative methods of valuation.
If less conservative methods of valuation were followed and lenders were to bring their appraisals more closely to the actual amount usefully expended by the builder the problem of the down payment would just about disappear. I want to emphasize that I deliberately use the words "the amount usefully expended" because I do not think there is any reason to include in the security expenditures which do not produce value. I contend that useful expenditures do produce value to an amount corresponding to the amount of those expenditures. I would suggest that the lending institutions should take greater note of the actual amount usefully expended in the building of a new dwelling rather than to rely solely on a process of estimation and experience.
Let us look at the case from another aspect. As I said a moment ago, the average estimated total cost of a single family dwelling in the second quarter of 1957 was $14,725 according to table 49. Even on the present loaning basis the loan ought to be $11,907.50 but the statistics show that the average loan is only $10,900; in other words, in the average case the loan is about $1,000 less than it ought to be. Having regard to the fact that the loan is insured under what I think are not ungenerous terms I believe the government would be well advised to examine further into the appraisal being made to see if they are not at the root of our present difficulties with regard to the down payment. I believe that more can be done to reduce the down payment by realistic appraisals than by changing the present ratio between the loan and the lending value.
I see that my time is running out, Mr. Chairman, and there are just two other points to which I should like to draw attention. The first is the phenomenal increase in the cost of land. Table 49 of the Canadian housing statistics for the second quarter of 1957 shows that for a single one-storey dwelling the land cost has increased from $523 in 1947 to $2,273 in the second quarter of 1957. This I think is very disquieting because the factor of the land costs makes homebuilding so difficult for people of modest resources and adds so much to the cost of the completed unit. I cannot help thinking that this is a factor which ought to receive serious consideration so as to see whether it would not be possible to reduce this element of the total cost and to determine what are the primary causes that make the cost of land such a large element of the total cost of a completed dwelling.
It does seem to me that perhaps land speculation is a cause and another cause may

National Housing Act
be the high cost of providing the local improvement services; but whatever may be the cause it is a subject which ought to receive close attention and I would suggest that the fullest inquiry into the matter should be undertaken either by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or some other competent body.
The second point I want to mention arises from the facts which appear in table 24 of the housing statistics which gives the range of the borrowers' incomes. The minister in his remarks the other night and indeed again today referred to the average income of borrowers under the National Housing Act and as reported at page 1878 of Hansard of December 4 said:
I was very much surprised to find that the qualifying income for the average National Housing Act loan made by approved lenders in the month of September of this year was $5,350. The average income for borrowers under the National Housing Act was $5,829.
The act and the present regulations undoubtedly encourage to a greater extent the building of homes for borrowers with higher incomes than for borrowers in the lower income brackets. Table 24 which I mentioned just a moment ago shows that of the 149,472 borrowers in the four years 1953 to 1956 inclusive all except 1,391 had incomes of $3,000 or more. In the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I ask if the time has not come for us to do something more for borrowers with incomes of less than $3,000. I cannot help thinking there would be a great deal to be said for a review both of the present standard of construction and of lending practices in connection with small homes. With such an objective in mind I feel it might be possible to design plans for homes which would be smaller and which would cost less than the average dwelling financed under the National Housing Act. I am convinced that by so doing we would be performing a useful service for a segment of the Canadian population which has perhaps not received as much attention as it deserves.
I fully realize, Mr. Chairman, that the statements I have just made in connection with the appraisals, in connection with the down payment and in connection with doing something for people in the income class under $3,000, might lend themselves to the question, why was this not done before? Well, Mr. Chairman, time does not permit me to deal with that question at all fully, but I think there is a good explanation. The observations that I have made, Mr. Chairman, have not been intended in any sense as being critical of actions of the government. I think it has not had adequate time to accomplish the changes that would have to be brought about

to meet with the objectives that I have just outlined, but I do think the suggestions merit consideration.
I know that my time has run out, Mr. Chairman, but I wonder whether I might have one or two minutes more?

In his remarks on the resolution itself, Mr. Chairman, the minister informed the committee of the intention of the government to amend the present regulations so as to raise the ratio of debt service to the home owners income from 23 per cent to 27 per cent. The 23 per cent, as hon. members will recall, translates into percentage figures the old adage that a man should not pay for his housing more per month than one week's salary. The proposed change would permit a borrower to qualify for home ownership with less income than that. Of course, the wisdom of making the change can only be determined by experience.
I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that this does not form part of the resolution and is essentially a matter for which the government alone must accept responsibility. But I hope the minister will note from table 24, to which I referred a moment ago, that the statistics show that the average debt service to income ratio in the six periods which the table covers has never once exceeded 19 per cent. Therefore, it may well be that the change in this figure may not be very significant. I appreciate the danger of arguing from averages; that is, from the general to the specific, and I merely wish to conclude on that point, Mr. Chairman, by saying that this is a matter of government responsibility and we are not called upon to express an opinion on it.
If I might conclude, Mr. Chairman, I would say that we favour the adoption of this resolution but I do hope that the points I have drawn to the attention of the minister, namely the need for more realistic appraisals, the cost of serviced land and the need to give more attention to home ownership for applicants in the lower income groups will receive the careful and solicitous attention of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have this opportunity to discuss this most important subject of housing at this session, more particularly in view of the rather disquieting answers we received to questions earlier in the session regarding legislation to amend the National Housing Act. I was most pleased to learn, irrespective of the manner in which the announcement was made, that notwithstanding the minister's answer to me on October 21, that the government did not

intend to bring down any amendment this session, they have seen fit to do so. I think the determination on the part of the members of this house, particularly the members from the opposition side, to stay on the job to discuss whatever legislation we could urge the government to bring down, is borne out by the fact that we are now discussing something which, in the earlier stages of this session, the government did not propose to bring down.
The previous speaker expressed a point of view which I think is definitely a little late in coming from a spokesman of that party, particularly in view of the fact that, as the hon. member pointed out, the cost of the average house under the National Housing Act had been going up year by year. Apparently the previous administration turned a deaf ear to pleas which we had made that some consideration be given to the Canadian citizens who are earning salaries less than $4,000 a year.
The C.C.F. position has been made clear on this matter over the years. We have called on the government to enact housing legislation to take care of the housing needs of all Canadians. We have argued that if priorities are to be given, then top priority should be given to Canadians in the lower income brackets. We find that the amendments to the National Housing Act which were passed in 1954 do not materially alter the situation. We still find the situation where, according to the minister's own figures, the average income increased over the years. For example, in 1955, the average income of a recipient of a loan under the National Housing Act was $5,023 per annum. In 1956, that had risen to $5,312. In the first quarter of 1957, it had risen to $5,615 and in the second quarter of 1957, to $5,829. The minister gave us a figure a few moments ago which indicated that in the third quarter of this year the average income had increased to $5,943. Therefore, the situation is becoming materially worse. The National Housing Act has tended to move farther away from the class of people whom we believe the housing legislation should serve first and foremost.
We in the C.C.F. have pointed out to the government that the ideal objective ought to be home ownership. It would be a very healthy situation in Canada if a great percentage of our people were to own their own houses. Certainly nothing has been done by the government in this legislation toward realizing that objective. However, apart from the home ownership provisions, we have always recognized the fact that there are a large number of Canadians who, because they receive incomes so low, irrespective of whatever provisions might be made in the National Housing Act for home ownership, would not
National Housing Act
be able to qualify. Then, again, there are sizeable numbers of Canadians who have jobs of a temporary nature and who are required occasionally to move from city to city for whom home ownership does not appeal. In order to serve the needs of that group of our population low-cost rental housing is the obvious answer. And yet, I recognize that there are provisions in certain sections of the National Housing Act with respect to limited dividend housing corporations and the like to provide so-called low rental housing; but there has not been too much activity in this field. Furthermore, the rents charged under no stretch of the imagination can be termed low.
The previous speaker referred to the general rule of thumb that a family is not able to, or should not be required to pay more than a week's salary, or roughly 20 per cent of their income for housing. What do we find? According to the statistics made available by the Department of National Revenue publication, Taxation Statistics of 1957, we note that of those making returns in Canada, whether they were taxable or non-taxable returns, 62 per cent of our people earned incomes of less than $3,000 a year. As a matter of fact, we know that there are well over a million and a half Canadians who earn incomes of less than $2,000 a year. If you accept the principle of one week's salary, or roughly one-fifth of the salary, as being the amount which a family can afford to spend on housing, then it is easy to see that if a person earns less than $3,000 a year he can hardly afford to pay more than $50 a month for rent. Those Canadians who earn less than $2,000 a year can hardly afford to pay more than $35 a month.
When we consider that this situation affects the majority of the people of Canada it is quite easy to see that the so-called low rental dwellings which have been made available are beyond the reach of the majority of the people of Canada. As a matter of fact, when the National Housing Act was amended in 1954 I referred to an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen at that time in which it was pointed out that a certain limited dividend housing corporation in the city of Ottawa, which was constructing so-called low cost housing, was charging rents well beyond the reach of a great percentage of the citizens of Ottawa.
Therefore, when the minister speaks of low cost housing, whether it be for home ownership or for rental purposes, I think we have to examine what he means by low cost housing, because certainly the type of housing which has been provided under certain sections of the National Housing Act has not resulted in rentals which the great percentage

National Housing Act
of the Canadian people can afford to pay. Thus, many of them are forced to live in substandard dwellings. The overcrowding that exists is something which must give us great cause for alarm.
It would appear obvious that the government ought to have given serious consideration to the whole question of low rental housing. I realize that in many instances the initiative is not being taken by municipalities simply because municipal taxes have reached such a high level in so many municipalities that they are loath to take any action which may conceivably bring about an increase in the mill rate, no matter how lofty the purpose may be. The result is that many municipalities with serious housing problems are not taking the initiative. In my opinion the fact that the sections under part II of the National Housing Act dealing with low rental housing have not been used nearly to the extent that might reasonably be hoped indicates the need for close attention on the part of the government to the provision of changes in the act to encourage a much faster rate of construction of low rental dwellings in Canada.
Apart from the question of low rental housing, with respect to which I realize the government can to some extent point the finger of blame at municipal bodies and provincial governments, there is, of course, the question of part I of the National Housing Act having to do with the encouragement of home ownership. Here again the statement we have made over the years that over 80 per cent of the people of Canada are unable to obtain any benefit whatsoever from the National Housing Act has been borne out by the statistics. As a matter of fact, the figure of 80 per cent which we have used was a little low. According to statistics issued by the Department of National Revenue, actually over 81.6 per cent of the people of Canada are earning incomes of less than $4,000 a year.
When we consider the average income of the recipient of a loan under the National Housing Act, we begin to realize the failure of the act to come to grips with the most important part of the problem. I appreciate the minister's concern about this matter. I note that in his statement on December 4 he said, as found at page 1880 of Hansard:
Quite frankly, I should like to be able to help an income group even lower than those who will be helped by this legislation.
I note that the minister is quite frank in admitting that the legislation does not provide for the low income groups. At another point in the minister's statement he referred to people in ordinary circumstances. In view of the statistics I have put on the record, I believe you can hardly describe people who

can qualify for a loan under the National Housing Act as being people in ordinary circumstances. It is true that their incomes might not be described as large but when you consider them as part of the general over-all population you realize they are people of more substantial means than the vast majority.
I also note that in his statement the minister pointed out that the amendments to be brought down in the bill will deal with the reduction of the down payment. This, of course, is something in which we have always been intensely interested. I think hon. members will recall that year in and year out we have advocated in the House of Commons a housing policy calling for a down payment of 10 per cent. But I would draw to the attention of the minister that along with our proposal to decrease the down payment to 10 per cent there was a companion recommendation that the interest rate should be reduced proportionately. If you reduce the down payment without at the same time reducing the interest payment you are going to add to the final cost of the house. While I recognize that under the circumstances it is most important to lower the down payment in order to include a larger group of people under the terms of the act, I can see no reason why the government did not take steps at this time to bring about a reduction in the interest rate.
I note the reference the minister made to the amendment to increase the amount of money which may be appropriated out of the consolidated revenue fund to be used by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in direct lending and that the amount is to be increased from $250 million to $400 million. Hon. members will recall that when the act was amended in 1954 the members of the C.C.F. group deplored the direction in which our housing legislation was moving. We pointed out with some alarm that the transfer of a greater measure of responsibility for housing from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation into the laps or to the tender mercies of the conventional lending institutions would bring about grave results, and indeed it has. I suggest that the very fact these amendments are being brought in today indicates an awareness on the part of the government that the private lending institutions have not measured up to the job which we expected them to do in 1954.
It is very difficult, as the hon. member who preceded me said, for housing to compete successfully in the money market with other forms of building and commercial ventures. In his statement the minister referred to the

trend towards larger loans and larger incomes on the part of recipients of loans under the National Housing Act. As found at page 1878 of Hansard he went on to say:
There is some reason for this trend because it is a good deal easier to handle a large loan than it is to handle a small one and I think some preference has been given by the different institutions to the larger loans.
Of course, that is the very point we tried to make in 1954, that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as a responsible agency of government seeking to deal with a social problem would be able to take cognizance of this fact and certainly would not give preference to those with higher incomes simply because it was more convenient or less trouble for them than to handle smaller loans. Yet, if we turn housing over to private enterprise how can we expect anything else than the very procedure which we have witnessed in recent years?
I suggest to the minister that it is the failure of the conventional lending institutions to provide the mortgage money needed for housing that has made this legislation necessary. Why this money was not made available is difficult to understand because, in the amendments brought down in 1954, there was an overly generous insurance provision which guaranteed the whole transaction at the expense of the borrower. Any risk, therefore, which would normally be involved in the lending of money was removed. It is very difficult to understand why sufficient money was not made available by the lending institutions to provide for this housing, if that is the problem as the minister suggests it is by the very fact this amendment seeks to increase the amount of money made available out of the consolidated revenue fund from $250 million to $400 million.
We are quite pleased to note that the government is putting greater reliance on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and is recognizing the fact that if we want to get the job done properly we have to take the responsibility ourselves for doing it. I suggest that the additional moneys made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will enable them to do a better job. Now, the amount involved of course is quite interesting. If we recognize the enormity of the problem facing the country at the present time, we begin to realize how little the amount is in terms of the general need. I note that the minister, in his statement of December 4, pointed out that of the additional moneys provided for by the amendment, $100 million would be taken up in loans on lower cost housing. He suggested that perhaps a lesser amount of from $50 million to $75 million 96698-158
National Housing Act
would be lent by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under other sections of the National Housing Act.
When we consider the tremendous need in this country for low rental housing, we realize how little is involved compared with the general over-all need. Unless the minister can assure the committee that the amount of money presently being made available by the conventional lending institutions will be maintained or increased, then it will simply mean we are going to increase the amount of money available for direct lending to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If the conventional lending institutions, under the insured plan, are going to reduce the amount they make available, then in the aggregate we are not going to be very much farther ahead. I believe this is something to which the members of the committee have to give careful consideration. I do not feel we can accept the assurances of the statement made by the minister that certain results are going to accrue from the passage of this resolution.
The hon. member who preceded me pointed out this very important question of the relationship of actual construction costs to the lending value placed on the dwelling. These two figures, of course, do not coincide and this involves an additional expense to be financed by the home purchaser. I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to the introduction of amendments that would bring the legislation in line with need. When I speak of "need" I am thinking in terms of the needs of people who are earning less than $3,000 or less than $3,500 a year.
The minister has stated that people can get a home with a down payment of $1,000 if they are earning $3,450 a year, but I think we will have to wait to see just how many people are able to get loans when they have incomes of $3,450. Even if we were to accept the results envisaged by the minister, we are still faced with the blunt fact that the majority of the people in Canada are excluded from the provisions of the National Housing Act. As a matter of fact, if one takes the $3,500 figure one finds that 73.1 per cent of the people of Canada earn less than $3,500 a year. Even if the legislation which the minister proposes to bring down is as good as he claims it is, it is still going to exclude almost three-quarters of the Canadian people.
I suggest that that is not good enough. I maintain that people who are earning incomes of only $3,000 or $2,000 a year are more in need of assistance under the housing act than any other group of Canadian people. I do not wish to trespass on the time of the committee, but I do want to refer briefly to the suggestion made by the hon. member

National Housing Act
for St. Antoine-Westmount concerning the part played by land costs. I mention this particularly in view of the fact that I have recently received a communication from the city council of the city of Regina in which they asked me to intercede with the government in order that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation regulations might be relaxed to the point where many areas in the city of Regina, now serviced with sewer and water and which are presently excluded from the lending provisions of the National Housing Act, might be included.
In my own city there are many people wishing to buy homes who are obliged to pay up to $2,000 for a lot. At the same time there are lots owned by the city of Regina which could be sold for $450 or $500, but which do not qualify under the regulations laid down by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. These lots, therefore, under the terms of the act, cannot be made available for housing. I would suggest to the minister that serious consideration be given to some modification in the regulations to permit those areas in my own city, which are serviced by sewers and water and which are presently beyond the pale so far as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is concerned, to be brought in at the earliest possible moment. This would make it possible to provide lower cost homes because the lots on which these houses would be built would cost much less than lots which might be purchased in other parts of the city.
Apart from the fact the legislation ignores the needs of at least 70 per cent of our people, the most glaring fault in the legislation is the failure of the government to do anything about interest rates. If people who want to buy homes under the National Housing Act are to be saddled with a tremendous debt brought about by excessively high interest rates, then of course the task of home ownership is going to be made that much more difficult. We in the C.C.F. have always argued that any reduction in the down payment should be accompanied by a reduction in interest rates. We feel that the failure of the government to introduce such a provision is the most serious flaw in the legislation coming before us. Therefore, in order to correct the situation, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That the resolution be amended by deleting the period after the word "payments" and by inserting at that point the following words: "and for a reduction in the rate of interest that may be charged by lenders under the act".
This resolution would then read, Mr. Chairman:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954 to increase from two hundred and fifty million dollars to four hundred million dollars the aggregate amount that
[Mr. Ellis.1
may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act; and also to provide for the reduction of down payments, and for a reduction in the rate of interest that may be charged by lenders under the act.

speechtext:
The
Minister of Public Works amazes me again. The amendment does not, in my submission, create or increase any charge on the government. The amendment suggests that there should be a change in the act reducing the amount of interest that may be charged by lenders under the act. That word "lenders" was chosen quite carefully in the drafting of this amendment, having in mind that in subsection 21 of section 2 of the National Housing Act there is this definition:
"Lender" means a loan, insurance, trust or other company or corporation, trustee of trust funds, building society, credit union or other co-operative credit society authorized to lend money on the security of real or immovable property and a bank.
The amendment makes no reference to additional government expenditure or to interest on money lent directly by the government. It refers only to money lent under the act by private lenders as defined in the legislation. There is in the act section 4 which gives the governor in council power by regulation to prescribe the maximum rate of interest and the formula is spelled out. I need not read it in full just now. The whole point, Mr. Chairman, is that this amendment has nothing to do with increasing the charge on the government in any way. It deals only with that section of the act which enables the government to fix a maximum rate of interest that the private lending institutions may charge.
I see the Minister of Public Works getting to the edge of his chair. If he has any other points, I shall be glad to deal with them. Perhaps while I am on my feet I might as well answer any point that might occur to him. It is perfectly correct, as the minister said, that a private member cannot move an amendment to a resolution of this kind if the private member's amendment involves a charge on the government. But this is an amendment that refrains from involving any charge on the government and is simply an

amendment under the terms of citation 440 of Beauchesne's third edition which reads as follows:
The fundamental terms of a money resolution submitted to the house with the Governor General's recommendation upon which a committee of the whole is set up cannot be amended. Amendments will only be in order if they fall within the terms of the resolution.
I might point out to the Minister of Public Works that I have before me two instances of amendments being moved to resolutions of this kind. Of course I have chosen my instances with care. In both cases the amendments were moved by Conservative members of the House of Commons. One case was only a short while ago. On April 16, 1956, there was before the committee of the whole a resolution preceding a bill to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act. The minister will recall that the subject under consideration was a certain 90 per cent provision. The Conservative members on the opposition side of the house were not satisfied with the way in which that 90 per cent provision was to be applied. The hon. member for Kamloops, now the Minister of Justice, moved:
That the resolution be amended by adding thereto after the words "not exceeding 10 per centum thereof" the following words:
"the portion of the highway to which such increased payment is to apply to be designated by the province."
That is found at page 2980 of Hansard of April 16, 1956. A question was raised as to whether this amendment was in order and this initial ruling was given by the deputy chairman, Mr. Applewhaite:
I might say that at the moment it does not appear to me that this proposed amendment would extend the financial commitment of the crown.
He made one or two other comments and then he said this:
However, at the moment, before asking the committee to vote, I would be willing to consider the matter further. At the moment I am not refusing to accept the amendment.
After three or four pages of debate, in which both substance and point of order are intermixed, Mr. Applewhaite returned to the matter as recorded at page 2986 and said this:
If the hon. member will permit me to interrupt I might say that there is a maximum provided in the resolution; that the aggregate of all expenditures under the act may be increased to a maximum of $250 million. Therefore I do not think it is possible for the amendment to increase the commitment. I have accepted the amendment.
Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?
The amendment was voted on. It was negatived by a vote of 74 to 38. The important point, Mr. Chairman, is that the present Minister of Justice-and I note with interest that he is now consulting the authorities-found it possible on that occasion to move an 96698-158i
National Housing Act
amendment to a resolution preceding a money bill, provided that it did not go beyond the financial commitment involved in the resolution itself.
The other instance that I have turned up goes back a number of years; but one must go back a number of years in order to find what happened when the Conservatives were last in power. I find that on March 29, 1932, Mr. Bennett had before the committee of the whole house a resolution preceding the bill concerning the unemployment and farm relief act of 1931. There had been an extended debate. This was one of those unhappy sessions in which closure had been used, and most of us in this house know what happens to tempers under that situation. But at any rate, when the house got into committee on the resolution preceding Mr. Bennett's bill it had become necessary, because of the passage of time, for the resolution to be amended. Let me admit readily that the amendment that was moved was proposed by another minister of the crown, namely by the then minister of justice, Mr. Guthrie, but Mr. Guthrie did not produce any royal recommendation for this amendment, arguing that it merely changed the terms of the resolution without increasing the financial commitment. There was a lengthy point of order debate in which such stalwarts as Mr. Mackenzie King, Mr. Ralston, Mr. Ian Mackenzie and others took part, with our late good friend Mr. R. B. Hanson in the chair as chairman of the committee of the whole house. But Mr. Hanson stood his ground that the amendment was in order and he used these words, as recorded at page 1505 of Hansard of March 29, 1932:

speechtext:
