Mr. Chairman, we in the province of British Columbia were rather pleased when the minister was appointed Minister of Public Works. We do not know what type of engineer he is going to be and how he will work out as Minister of Public Works. However, with regard to the matter of housing, a subject which is of such vital concern, the people of British Columbia will always have a most sympathetic and understanding man as minister.
We have arrived at a time when we have to take a look at what is happening in the field of housing. For some years we had considerable difficulty with the former minister in that he continually refused to acknowledge that a serious situation was beginning to develop nationally from the point of view of housing shortage. For an explanation of that attitude on the part of the then government we have to look at a statement made by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe on February 13 of this year when he was reported as having said that the record suggested that we had been building more houses in Canada in the last few years than the current rate of family growth in the country appeared to warrant. I believe he had reached the conclusion that it would be in the best interests of the country if there was a slow-down in the rate of house construction, and that was rather evident from the policies that were being pursued.
I do not wish to indicate any opposition whatsoever to the resolution but I should like to examine the National Housing Act to some extent. I should like to pay tribute to the work that has been accomplished under the provisions of the act over the years. I hate to think of what kind of housing situation we would be faced with if the former government had not initiated the act, in 1945 I believe. I should also like to pay tribute to the officials. I feel that within the limits of their powers they have in the main done whatever they were able to do to make the act a success.
However, I do submit that the National Housing Act has not met the housing needs of the Canadian people. We have only to look at the statistics to see that that is so. We find that since 1945 there has been a growth of 4,517,000 in Canada's population. That indicates an approximate need for one and one-third million new housing units. I submit that that number is far in excess of the number of new housing units built since the war. I believe we have approached the million mark but we have not anywhere met the needs of our growth in population. I have here housing bulletin No. 35 of the Vancouver housing association dated October, 1957. It deals with the local scene and in the first paragraph they say:
According to provincial government estimates, the population of B.C. increased by 88,500 people or over 6 per cent during the year ended June 30, 1957. At 3J persons per household, this means a requirement of some 25,000 housing units. During this period 15,000 dwellings were completed, indicating a shortage of no less than 10,000 units in a single year.
This year there has been heavy immigration into Canada. I have the annual report here and it indicates that 164,856 people entered

Canada in 1956. I believe that the figures for 1957 will show that over 200,000 people have come to this country. If anyone cares to dispute what I have said, let me submit the problem to another test which to my mind is the acid test of whether the housing shortage is becoming worse or is being alleviated. I refer to the level of rents. I believe that the shortage of homes determines the level of rents, and we have not seen any major reduction of rentals since the war. The general movement of rentals has been upward and in my opinion that indicates beyond doubt that the situation is becoming worse instead of better.
The hon. member for Regina City went to some length to explain that the act has failed us in another respect. It has failed us in that the wrong people are receiving help from the government. I was very pleased to hear the minister express his sentiments when he indicated that he was most concerned about enabling people with low incomes to obtain housing accommodation. I submit to the minister that in the main the act has completely failed the people of Canada in this regard ever since it was first initiated.
I know that the theory can be put forward that if a rich man builds a home he moves out of his old home and therefore another housing unit has been made available so why should we worry about who gets the new home. To me that represents the philosophy of the crumbs falling from the table and the little people getting the crumbs, a philosophy to which I cannot subscribe. I think even the minister will agree that when the revenue of the government of Canada and the taxation of the nation are used to supply housing a responsible government will make every effort to make sure that government action will be the instrument to help those who really need help and that the National Housing Act should not be used to assist in the building of homes for people who can go to orthodox financial institutions and arrange their own financing. Where do the two-thirds of our people in the lower income category obtain money in order to secure housing? In order to show how serious the situation is I should like to place on the record a few advertisements taken from the Vancouver Sun of Saturday, December 14. Under "Money Wanted"; we find:
First mortgage 7 per cent, $3,250 buys $4,000 at $45 a month.
Farther down, there is another ad:
First mortgage, $2,000 bonus, $5,050 buys $7,050 first mortgage payable at $71.50 per month, 7 per cent.
Then, there is the address where you apply. There has been a long list of these advertisements for first mortgages at 7 per cent or
National Housing Act
more which are being discounted at 25 per cent or more, and second mortgages are worse. I have a letter here in which a man informs me that to get a second mortgage of $1,500 he signed a second mortgage for $2,000; he paid a bonus of $300; he paid a commission of $200, and he paid lawyer's fees of $38. There was paid out to him a net payment of $1,492. The interest rate was 7 per cent. I was very interested in noting that the terms of repayment were $61 per month. In other words, there was only a three-year agreement. Now, the ordinary people of Canada are being taken for a ride, a harsh ride and one that they can ill afford.
Here we have the government of Canada spending hundreds of millions of dollars a year on housing and that money is not being made available to these poor people who are in such desperate need. I realize the minister would like to limit discussion on this resolution because he believes the matter is rather urgent. However, he is asking for an increase in the capitalization of this institution, and I feel that subject is weighty enough. The minister himself has indicated that at a later date he hopes to bring in a broad revision of the act and therefore a detailed reaction of the members of the house at this time might serve a useful purpose by making sure that when the complete revision of the act does come it will contain something that will be really worth while for the Canadian people. Food, clothing and shelter, we say, are the prime necessities of life. In dealing with housing, one is dealing with shelter and I think this debate is just as important as any wheat debate in this house.
The economy of my province depends very heavily on a prosperous housing industry. Not only is our population growing at such a rapid rate, largely because of immigration into the province that we have a housing need, but also, Mr. Chairman, half of our people earn their living directly from the lumbering industry. At the present time we have much more than our share of the unemployed of our nation. There is nothing of which I can think that is as helpful in relieving unemployment as a real shot in the arm for our housing industry.
The resolution, Mr. Chairman, calls for an increase in the amount of money allotted under section 22 of the act from $250 million to $400 million. I should like to say to the minister that I believe this committee would have welcomed the raising of that amount even higher. I see no reason why it should necessarily be limited to $400 million. After all, $400 million accounts for only 40,000 houses, in effect, and we are today building each year 100,000 fewer houses than our

National Housing Act
nation really needs. We in this group have long advocated the establishment of a national investment board which would look after such social needs as housing.
However, if the minister feels that he cannot go along with that, might I recommend to him that a national housing bond issue be made. I noted that the other day the Minister of Finance did not have any difficulty at all in having the latest Canada savings bond issue oversubscribed. As the hon. member for Regina City said, we should make some move to lower the interest rate to those who need homes. The issuance of a national housing bond series at' 3J per cent I feel would make a billion dollars available. The government might then turn around and let the people who need this money most have it at cost.
I feel the minister might also investigate whether or not greater use could be made of the credit union movement. Lately this movement has, because of the need of its members, gone to great lengths in supplying housing money across the country. I feel the movement has now reached the age and gained the experience which would warrant the government granting it more recognition and making greater use of this medium. It is obvious that private sources of mortgage money at modest interest rates are disappearing. They have been disappearing ever since 1951, ever since the great expansion in our industrial empire began to take place. The insurance companies and the mortgage companies have shown less and less interest in supplying the money needed in the housing field. I recall when the former government brought the banks into the housing field. They did this for an excellent reason, and the reason was that the insurance and mortgage companies were rapidly leaving the field. The banks had to be brought in because apparently at that time they were the only source available of investment money.
At that time we in this group warned the government of the day that bank investments in the field of housing would last only so long, and then would level off. Today the banks, in the main, are only investing in housing the mortgage money that is repaid, and they are only investing that percentage in housing that has a relationship to the growth of the assets of the bank. Once again we have reached the end of the rope. Some day the government will have to realize that unless they are going to exert some pressure on the existing institutions they will have to take over this responsibility of supplying money.
I was not very happy, Mr. Chairman, with the answer the minister gave to the question

asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I believe the question referred to the fees paid to approved lenders by the government when they handle government money. The minister read out a table of fees from an agreement. I am not going to argue with that reply. However, if the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway did not mean to ask this question, I mean to ask it. When the government supplies money to an approved lending institution at 3| per cent or 4 per cent-we do not know what the rate is-how is it that the lending institution in turn can charge the purchaser of a home 6 per cent? I never before knew of a table of fees. I hope the minister is going to reply to this question. Does the lending institution receive 2 per cent or 2J per cent on the handling of government money and, in addition to that, receive a fixed fee as well? If that is so, I feel that there is something wrong.

speechtext: In other words, I take it that this $150 million which the minister made available some months ago did not involve the use of the scale of fees?

What I want to know is this. What happens when I go to the Bank of

Montreal and obtain a National Housing Act loan. The minister has told us that he is now supplying this money to the extent of $150 million because they were unwilling to lend on, or did not have any more money to devote to housing. I take it they are getting that money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for 4 per cent, or as the minister says 4| per cent. Yet I as a purchaser must pay 6 per cent. Then the minister says in addition to that there is a scale of fees.

I know that after I finished grade three arithmetic I went to grade four and then to grade five. Let us see if we can get a little bit more information. To my way of thinking 4| per cent plus jj of one per cent plus i of one per cent do not add up to 6 per cent yet. The thing I want to point out is this. In 1953 I took rather severe objection to the handling of government money as the situation existed prior to that provision, in that N.H.A. loans were supplied, 75 per cent by the lending institutions and 25 per cent by the government at that time. Government money was made available at cost to the lending institution. The lending institution added profit into that interest rate which was charged to the purchaser. That procedure, as the minister knows, was abolished when we amended the act.
At present we are again entering an era apparently where government money is being handed over or lent to the lending institutions. What I want to make sure of is this. I must say that the lending institutions and the banks especially have done recently a most remarkable job. The banks have reached many thousands of people in Canada which the lending institutions prior to that time refused to deal with. However, what I want to make sure of is that these institutions are not making a rake-off on the Canadian people's money and on these National Housing Act loans. If people lend out their own money, that is an entirely different matter from that of using the taxpayer's money for that purpose. I hope that later on we can get a little bit clearer answer to that question.
I have noted in the past considerable condemnation of municipal governments for their failures to take advantage of the provisions of the National Housing Act. I feel that in the 96698-159
National Housing Act
main these criticisms have been most unwarranted. I hope the minister, by means of regulation if he does not want to amend the act in that respect, will see whether things cannot be made much more attractive to our municipal governments across the country.
The hon. member for Regina City spoke of lots selling at $2,000 and said he thought that was an extremely high price. The minister knows full well that the average modest National Housing Act lot in his community and in mine is in price away over and beyond the $2,000 which the hon. member for Regina City thought was very expensive. If the municipal governments were given a little bit more encouragement I feel that many more of them would make lots available at a much more modest price.
The minister spoke of the down payment and he is also amending the regulations so that those devoting 27 per cent of their income towards meeting payments will be eligible. I think the minister was slightly contradictory on December 4 when he was asserting that this change in regulations would make more people eligible because, only a few sentences ahead of that, he admitted that naturally when you lower the down payment there is a larger amount owing and therefore the monthly payments are higher. Therefore, unless we amend the regulations, we shall be eliminating an even larger share of low income people. I just wonder why the 27 per cent was arrived at. Is the difference between 23 per cent and 27 per cent the percentage that is needed to keep the minimum income requirements at the same level as it was previously, or has there been any extra allowance in this change of the regulation? If that is so, then we might be guilty of misleading the people if we say that now more of them will be eligible because of this amendment.
The lowering of the interest rate proposed by the hon. member for Regina City would reduce the cost and would make more people eligible. I think that the principle is sound, as did the hon. member who preceded me. He pointed out a number of instances in which government money is being made available for all kinds of other interests in our nation at a lower rate. After all, housing is one of the basic needs of our Canadian people and there is no valid reason why this government should make loans to pipe line companies or any other industrial enterprise at a rate lower than that which the people of Canada are obliged to pay for housing.
I know that, if certain people had their way there would be a great deal of money available in the housing field. There is a very simple answer to the problem and that is to allow the interest rate to shoot away up high.
I hope that is not going to be the philosophy

National Housing Act
that this government will adopt, namely that in order to obtain this money they will have to raise interest rates so high that they begin to compete with industrial enterprise in our country. I think those days are gone forever.
I should like to make just a few proposals.
I think the minister's regulations need amending in such a way that no man continuing to live in the same community can become eligible more than once for N.H.A. approved loans. I have witnessed considerable speculation on the part of people earning a fair income who, being very eligible for an N.H.A. approved loan, will move into a new home and the minute they have moved in the house is listed for sale. They bide their time and they can make a few thousand dollars, and they then move out of that house and in a new N.H.A. approved-loan home.
I think that is something into which the minister might well look; I think it is an abuse for which this act was never intended.
I wish the minister would also order a comparison to be made as to why houses built under veterans legislation enterprises are so much more successful in meeting the real needs of the people than are those built under the National Housing Act legislation. I think there are many features of the veterans housing from which we might take a lesson.
